title: Secrets: never in a script, never in a file
summary: SecretManagement and SecretStore: register a vault, store and read secrets, PSCredential and SecureString, and where secrets live in CI and on servers.

steps.title: Where secrets go wrong
body: Tokens and passwords leak in boring ways: committed in a script, pasted in a config file, printed in a log,
left in `$history`, passed on a command line that `ps` (or Task Manager) shows to everyone on the machine. The
rules:
1. **Never in the script or the repo.** Not even "temporarily". Git history is forever, and secret scanners
(GitHub's, your company's) will find it after the attacker does.
2. **Not in a plain file** if you can avoid it: anyone with a backup, a copy of the disk or the same account reads it.
3. **Get it at run time from a secret store**, keep it in a `SecureString` or `PSCredential` as long as you can, and
never write it to output or logs.
**SecretManagement** (`Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretManagement`) is one set of commands for many stores
("vaults"): `Get-Secret`, `Set-Secret`, `Get-SecretInfo`, `Remove-Secret`. Vault extensions plug in behind it:
| Vault module | Stores secrets in |
| `Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretStore` | an encrypted file in your profile (any OS) |
| `Az.KeyVault` | Azure Key Vault |
| `SecretManagement.KeePass`, `SecretManagement.1Password`, ... | community vaults for password managers |
The script only ever says `Get-Secret -Name OpsApiToken`; which vault answers is configuration.

steps.prompt: Acceptable for a production API token, or not?
items: The pipeline's secret variable, read from an environment variable
`$token = 'abc123'` at the top of the script
`-Token abc123` on the command line of a scheduled task
Azure Key Vault through `Get-Secret` with the Az.KeyVault vault
steps.explain: Command lines are visible to other users of the machine and land in logs; verbose output lands in job logs. In CI, the platform's secret variables (masked in logs) are the store; on servers, a vault the job's identity can read.

steps.title: SecretStore in practice
body: ```powershell
Install-PSResource Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretManagement, Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretStore   # once (installed here)
Register-SecretVault -Name LocalStore -ModuleName Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretStore -DefaultVault
Set-Secret -Name OpsApiToken -Secret (Read-Host 'Token' -AsSecureString)    # typed, not echoed
Get-SecretInfo                                       # names and types, never values
$token = Get-Secret -Name OpsApiToken                # a SecureString
Invoke-RestMethod $uri -Authentication Bearer -Token $token
Get-Secret -Name OpsApiToken -AsPlainText            # when an API only takes a string header
SecretStore normally asks for a **password** to unlock the store (for a while, `PasswordTimeout`). An unattended
job cannot type one, so service accounts often use `Set-SecretStoreConfiguration -Authentication None`: then the
store is protected **only by the account's own files** (on Windows, the user's DPAPI key). That is better than a
plain file, but a full secret manager (Key Vault with a managed identity, for example) is the stronger choice for
production servers. This machine's store is already configured that way, without a vault registered.

steps.title: Move the API token into a vault
prompt: `~/scripts/ticket-count.ps1` reads its token from `~/.config/ops/api-token`. Move it into SecretManagement:
1. register a SecretStore vault named **`LocalStore`** as the default vault;
2. store the token (without its trailing newline) as a secret named **`OpsApiToken`**;
3. change the script to get the token with `Get-Secret`, so it still prints `tickets: 47`;

checks.name: LocalStore is the default vault
checks.fail: `Get-SecretVault` should show `LocalStore`, backed by `Microsoft.PowerShell.SecretStore`, as the default vault.

checks.name: OpsApiToken holds the token
checks.fail: `Get-Secret OpsApiToken -AsPlainText` should return exactly the token (no newline at the end).

checks.name: the script works from the vault
no token file, no token or file path in the script
checks.fail: Delete `~/.config/ops/api-token`, and make the script use `Get-Secret` instead of the file.

hints: In the script: `$token = Get-Secret -Name OpsApiToken -AsPlainText`. Then `Remove-Item ~/.config/ops/api-token`.
explain: The script is now safe to commit and share, and rotating the token is one `Set-Secret` with no code change. On a
Windows server the same script can run against an Azure Key Vault by registering that vault under the same name.
One more leak to close: PowerShell's own history. `Set-Secret -Secret (Read-Host -AsSecureString)` keeps the value
out of `(Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath`; PSReadLine also skips lines that look like they contain secrets.

steps.prompt: A function needs a user name and password to log in to an appliance. What should its parameter be?
steps.explain: A `PSCredential` carries the user name and a `SecureString` password together, works with `Get-Credential` and `Get-Secret` (which can store a whole credential), and is what PSScriptAnalyzer expects. Inside, `$Credential.GetNetworkCredential().Password` gets the plain text at the last moment, only if an API truly needs it.
